The problem in one line (judges already know it)

“Help a retail chain choose the best location for its next store using AI, and explain why.” We say this once and move on.

Numbers you can quote

15,350real places used6,541hexagon zones5business types 9AI parts working17product features6.9 Mpeople covered

Before you present

  • Fill the yellow brackets on the team slide: who built what, and one sentence on mentor feedback. We did not invent these.
  • Check the claim “first prototype ran on made-up data” matches what you showed in Evaluation 1. Change it if not.
  • Start both servers (run-backend.bat, run-frontend.bat) and open http://localhost:5173. Do one practice search so the data is warm.
  • Pick Pharmacy for the demo: it uses all the learned models. Do not start with Sports (it uses the simple method).
  • Practise once with a timer. If you run long, shorten the technology part, not the demo.

The script

0:00 – 0:25OpeningSpeaker 1 · 52 words · about 26 s
SAYGood morning. We are Team SiteSense from Walchand College of Engineering. Our problem statement is simple: help a retail chain choose the best place for its next store, using AI. Today we will show what we built since the last evaluation, how it works, and what comes next for the final submission.
DOStay on the home screen. No clicking yet.
0:25 – 1:20Progress since Evaluation 1Criterion 1: Development progress (10 marks)Speaker 2 · 126 words · about 63 s
SAYFirst, our progress. Our first prototype ran on made-up city data. Since then we have rebuilt it on real data. We now use more than 15 thousand real places from OpenStreetMap, like shops, offices, hospitals, bus stops and roads. We add real population data from WorldPop, about seven million people. We split Pune into six and a half thousand small hexagon zones, and we measure what surrounds each one. The app now covers five business types: sports, food, fashion, pharmacy and electronics. Nine AI parts are working, from ranking to profit simulation to explanations. We also redesigned the screen so a shop owner can follow every step. And everything about a city or a business now lives in a simple settings file, not in the code.
DOOpen the 4 Data & trust tab and point to the pipeline list and the counts.

SAYNow the demo. I choose what I sell: pharmacy. I can set limits like budget or rent, or I can simply type a sentence in the Just ask box. Then I press Find best locations. In a few seconds the map shows how good every area is. Darker means a better match. The numbered pins are the top five sites.
DOClick Pharmacy, then Find best locations. Point at the map, the pins and the strip that shows how the city was narrowed down.

SAYHere is site number one, near Deccan Gymkhana. It shows the expected profit as a range: a weak case, a likely case and a strong case. We never give one made-up number. On the right we explain why: many helpful businesses nearby, an affluent area, and room for another store. Below that we show the risks, a confidence level, and why this site beats number two. Every figure is labelled real or estimated.
DOClick pin 1. Point at Why this area, What could go wrong and the confidence note.
2:30 – 2:55Demo 3: what-ifCriterion 3: DemonstrationSpeaker 3 · 49 words · about 24 s
SAYNext, what-if. If rents rise thirty percent, we re-run everything. Profits fall, and sites two and three swap places. An owner can also drop a new rival on the map. And if you add your own stores, we estimate how much a new store would take sales from them.
DOOpen 2 What-if, move the slider to +30%, press Run the what-if.
2:55 – 3:20Demo 4: expansion planCriterion 3: DemonstrationSpeaker 3 · 44 words · about 22 s
SAYLast in the demo, the expansion plan. For three stores, the planner picks the best group together, so the stores do not steal each other's customers. The Data and trust page shows where every number comes from, and how well each model was tested.
DOOpen 3 Expansion plan, press Build the plan. Then flash the model-score table on the Data & trust tab.
3:20 – 4:20Technology and problem solvingCriterion 2: Technical quality (10 marks)Speaker 4 · 126 words · about 63 s
SAYNow the technology. The front end is React with TypeScript and a Leaflet map. The back end is Python with FastAPI. For AI we use XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost, SHAP for explanations, and Google OR-Tools to plan several stores. We solved real problems along the way. The map data server kept failing, so we added retries and saved copies of the data. Our first profit numbers were too high, so we recalibrated the simulation. To stop the model from cheating, we hide the chain shops it learns from, and we test it on whole neighbourhoods it has never seen. Where data is too thin, like sports shops, the app says so and uses a simpler method. We also added tests, input checks and clear error messages.
DOPoint at the architecture picture on the slide (or the overview PDF, page 5).

SAYOur team shared the work. [NAME 1] built the data pipeline. [NAME 2] built the models. [NAME 3] built the interface. [NAME 4] handled testing and documents. Following mentor feedback, we [ONE SENTENCE: what you changed].
DOFill the square brackets before presenting. Each member says their own part in one sentence.

If the judges ask (short answers)

Q. Is the data real?
The map data is real (OpenStreetMap, 15,350 places) and so is the population (WorldPop). Property prices, margins and spending per person are our own estimates, and the app labels them as estimates.
Q. Where does the profit number come from?
From a simulation of shoppers choosing between stores by distance and attractiveness, repeated 300 times with uncertain inputs. We have no real sales data, so it is decision support, not a guarantee.
Q. How do you know the AI works?
We tested on whole neighbourhoods the model never saw. It finds chain-like locations much better than population alone, for example pharmacy 52% against 8% (Data & trust page). That shows it finds proven-looking sites, not proof of profit.
Q. Why does Sports use a simpler method?
Only 25 sports shops are mapped in OpenStreetMap for Pune, so there are too few examples to learn from. The app says this and lowers its confidence.
Q. Is this just a chatbot?
No. The AI does the analysis: ranking, simulation and explanations. The Just ask box only reads the request and fills the form; it never writes the answers.
Q. What are the limits?
Study area is a rectangle, not the exact city border; the growth data was unavailable at build time; rent model is basic; no zoning or online-demand data.
Q. What will you do next?
Exact city border, real sales from one chain to calibrate, live rent listings, deployment online, reports and accounts.
